item.title: Xi to pay state visit to US from Sept 23 to 25
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-21
Xi to pay state visit to US from Sept 23 to 25 BEIJING -- President Xi Jinping will pay a state visit to the United States from Sept 23 to 25 at the invitation of US President Donald Trump, a Chinese foreign ministry spokesman announced on Monday. During the visit, Xi and Trump will have an in-depth exchange of views on major issues concerning China-US relations and world peace and development, Chinese foreign ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun said at a regular news briefing. Head-of-state diplomacy plays an irreplaceable role in providing strategic guidance for China-US relations, and the exchange of visits between the two heads of state within six months marks a historic milestone, Guo said. China is ready to work with the US side to enrich the connotation of the constructive relationship of strategic stability, enhance dialogue and cooperation, properly manage differences, and continuously contribute to the well-being of both peoples and global peace, stability and prosperity, he added.

item.title: Southwest China taps acoustics of its karst landscapes
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-21
In a cave in Guilin, Guangxi Zhuang autonomous region, sound-healing practitioner Xiong Liying gently strikes the rim of a singing bowl with a soft mallet, and a clear, bell-like note rises from the bowl. As she circles the mallet steadily around its rim, the note swells into a long, even hum. However, the bowls are only part of what Xiong listens to. Near the cave entrance, rain patters on leaves and wind moves through the foliage. Deeper inside, drops of water fall intermittently from the rock above. "They fall from different heights and in different places, so each one can make a different sound," Xiong said. "Sometimes a drop falling into a metal vessel sounds different from one landing in a ceramic bowl, while the size and shape of the container can alter the note further." For some young urban dwellers, the experience offers a moment to turn inward. Chen Shiyu, a Shanghai resident who has been attending singing bowl sessions for the past two months, said: "Life in a big city moves fast. I'm constantly trying to keep up with work and everything else. But as soon as I hear the bowl, I feel grounded. My breathing slows down, and although I'm still aware of everything around me, I feel peaceful inside." In Southwest China, where extensive karst landscapes are home to many caves, underground rivers and striking rock formations, sound is becoming another way to experience these subterranean spaces. Long visited for their visual spectacle, some caves are now being explored not only as places to see, but also as places to listen and reflect. In Guizhou province, the sounds were not quite as calming, and the music scene was literally underground when the annual Colorful Guizhou Cave Music Week returned to Shuanghe Cave in Suiyang county for its fourth season. Performances spanning traditional, rock and electronic music were staged inside the cave, where organizers have developed "cave + music" alongside other experiential tourism activities. Similar experiments have appeared elsewhere. In Yunnan province, a five-day cave coffee concert held in Lushui during the May Day holiday combined live music with a space already used for coffee, local culture and other tourism experiences. In Guiyang, Guizhou, Liu Junliang and his team have been exploring a similar relationship between sound and stone through live concerts. As the opening notes of The Ivory Tower, an instrumental piece by Japanese composer Takashi Kako, sounded inside a limestone cave, they struck the surrounding rock and returned across the chamber. Some echoes came back almost immediately, while others seemed to linger deeper inside the cave. Even after the musicians stopped, Wang Xiaocui, head of the orchestra, could still hear them. "As performers, we feel that very strongly." Liu said: "Listening to music is already enjoyable and romantic. I thought that if we moved it into a cave, with the lighting and the natural surroundings, it could create a completely different atmosphere." Wang said that, after the concert, "I could see smiles on the audience's faces, and people naturally connecting with one another. Beyond costs and returns, bringing joy to so many people is what makes the project truly rewarding for us."

item.title: A 'naughty child' warming the world
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-21
A 'naughty child' warming the world El Niño, meaning "little boy" in Spanish, is an innocuous name for a geographical phenomenon that can make half the world swelter while sending the other half scrambling for sandbags to control floods. The name has an interesting origin. Centuries ago, fishermen off the northern coast of Peru noticed that around Christmas, a southward warm current appeared near shore, briefly reversing the usual cold flow. It usually brought tropical fish rarely seen in those waters and occasional rainfall that briefly turned the desert green. The warm current was named El Niño after the Christ child. Don't let the name fool you. El Niño is anything but small. It involves prolonged periods of unusually warm sea-surface temperatures across the central and eastern equatorial Pacific. Meteorologists have fairly strict criteria for defining an El Niño event: sea-surface temperatures in a key monitoring region of the tropical Pacific must remain at least 0.5 degrees Celsius above average for five consecutive overlapping three-month periods. The stronger the temperature anomaly, the stronger the El Niño is generally considered to be. The next "little boy" may be particularly troublesome. Forecasts suggest that by the end of 2026, the tropical Pacific could be heading toward an exceptionally strong El Niño, potentially rivaling the most powerful events on record. Another reason for concern is the tropical Pacific's role as a giant ocean battery. Before El Niño arrives, heat accumulates beneath the surface, as if the battery were charging. Once enough energy has built up, it discharges, releasing heat into the atmosphere and triggering a chain reaction. By August 2026, the tropical Pacific had accumulated an extraordinary amount of heat, surpassing levels seen during some previous record-setting El Niño events. El Niño does not recognize borders. As the Pacific gets warmer, it sends ripples through the atmosphere that disturb weather patterns thousands of kilometers away. The most immediate impact is higher temperatures, with the warmest year often occurring several months after El Niño peaks. This pattern was evident following the El Niño that began in late 2023. It contributed to the record warmth of 2024, which was the warmest year in recorded history. Adding another, even bigger El Niño to an already warming planet raises the baseline for extreme weather. A hotter atmosphere holds more moisture — roughly 7 percent more for every 1 degree Celsius of warming. That is a cruel multiplier. Wet regions may experience torrential rain, while dry places lose water faster through evaporation. Floods and droughts then become two sides of the same warming coin. El Niño often divides the world this way. In parts of Southeast Asia and eastern Australia, it can lead to heat and drought. On the eastern side of the Pacific, the script reverses. Peru and Ecuador may face unusually heavy rain, causing floods and landslides. Even the Atacama Desert, one of the driest places on Earth, can bloom after unusual rainfall, turning a barren landscape into a surreal carpet of flowers. The ecological consequences can be profound. El Niño-related changes in rainfall and temperature have been associated with conditions favorable to major locust outbreaks across East Africa and parts of Asia, threatening crops and food security on a vast scale. In China, El Niño effects can vary. During the development of an El Niño event, parts of the middle Yangtze region can turn drier, while the following summer could witness persistent heavy rain and flooding along the Yangtze River and in southern China. However, El Niño is not a crystal ball. It raises the odds of extremes but does not dictate specific outcomes in a city, river basin or province. Other factors, such as monsoons, ocean temperatures in the Indian Ocean, Arctic sea ice, snow over the Qinghai-Xizang Plateau and atmospheric circulation in the mid — and high latitudes also influence outcomes. Climate is not a single switch but a complex system with many moving parts. The critical question is whether global warming is making El Niño more extreme. While the science is still evolving and climate models do not agree on every detail, there is a consensus that a warmer world is likely to increase the variability and severity of extreme El Niño events. Climate change may not turn every El Niño into a super El Niño, but it is raising the temperature of the room in which the "little boy" is playing — and making his tantrums potentially more damaging. This shifts the focus from disaster relief to proactive resilience-building. Cities need drainage systems designed for heavier downpours, better water storage for extended dry spells, cooler urban layouts and stronger infrastructure. Rural areas need resilient irrigation and drainage systems, adaptable cropping patterns and crops better able to withstand drought and flooding. Since El Niño is a global phenomenon, resilience efforts cannot stop at national borders. A drought in one region can disrupt food prices elsewhere, while floods can damage supply chains thousands of kilometers away. Ecological disasters can become economic or security issues long before they reach another country's shores. That makes international cooperation more than an act of goodwill. Countries need to share climate and ocean data, coordinate responses to extreme weather, strengthen global food-supply chains and help vulnerable nations prepare before disaster strikes. The super El Niño looming over 2026 and 2027 should not be seen as nature's punishment. It is a warning about the kind of world we are entering. Climate stability, once taken for granted, now requires active defense. We may never be able to keep the "little boy" from causing trouble. But we can build a house strong enough to withstand his tantrums. The author is a researcher at the Institute of Atmospheric Physics at the Chinese Academy of Sciences. item.title: NEV brands eye bright export future
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-21
NEV brands eye bright export future Chinese firms make green transition more affordable and achievable BEIJING — Carlos Alberto Corro Martin used to work for Ebro, an iconic brand of Spain's auto sector that had once faded into memory after its factories fell silent and jobs disappeared. In 2024, with Chinese automaker Chery partnering with Spanish automaker EV Motors, the legendary brand was revived. Electric models rolled off production lines, creating some 1,000 local jobs. "I'm very happy to see it return to the market," said Corro Martin, now a Chery dealer. "I believe the cooperation can open even broader prospects for the Spanish auto industry." Supported by battery technology advantages, intelligent systems and supply-chain efficiency, Chinese new energy vehicle brands are not just winning the hearts of global consumers, but also generating greater spillovers beyond market expansion — creating local jobs, supporting industrialization, and making the green transition more affordable and achievable. In the first eight months, China's total auto exports reached 7.153 million units, up 66.7 percent, including 3.435 million NEVs, a 1.2-fold increase, according to the China Association of Automobile Manufacturers. Rather than simply shipping cars, many Chinese automakers are building manufacturing and research facilities overseas. In South Africa, Chery inaugurated a manufacturing plant in Rosslyn in July, retaining all 692 employees, with expectations of creating nearly 3,000 jobs across the supply chain. "Chery's investment will pave the way for technology transfer, automation, digitalization and advanced manufacturing systems," said South African Deputy President Paul Mashatile, adding that these developments will strengthen South Africa's industrial capacity. In Brazil, Chinese automaker BYD is embedding research and development, production, sales, services and supply chains into the local economy. Its plant in the state of Bahia employed 5,500 direct workers as of July this year, 86 percent of them from Bahia. Once fully operational, it is expected to support 20,000 direct and indirect jobs, with the company aiming for local suppliers to account for over 50 percent of components by 2027. The expanding footprints of overseas investment come along with the increasing popularity of Chinese NEVs across diverse markets. In Europe, new-car registrations of Chinese brands have for two consecutive months surpassed those of Japanese automakers. In Southeast Asia, consumers in Thailand and Singapore have queued for popular Chinese NEV models, while in the Middle East, Chinese brands have continued to gain traction even amid regional instability. Chinese automakers are also tailoring vehicles to local demands. Chery, now present in over 130 countries and regions, has optimized acceleration and hill-climbing for South America's mountains and strengthened interior sealing for the Middle East's deserts. Chinese NEV brands are especially gaining market share in the Middle East, Africa, Southeast Asia and other parts of the Global South, according to Ron Zheng, senior partner of Roland Berger and Asia head of automotive practice. "For consumers in these emerging markets, Chinese NEVs are not only affordable, but also offer superior features," Zheng said. In Malaysia, Zeekr, the premium NEV brand under Chinese automaker Geely, entered the market in December 2024. Within months, Zeekr vehicles were more visible on Malaysian roads. "Previously, Malaysians may have associated Chinese cars mainly with affordability," said Zarul Fadzly, sales manager for Zeekr's KLCC and Johor Bahru outlets. "But with the entry of Zeekr and other Chinese brands, they have experienced firsthand the safety, performance and quality of the vehicles. Their perception has changed. Now they are more inclined to pursue the performance and quality of Chinese brands." On the broader impact of Chinese brands entering Malaysia, Fadzly added: "They bring more advanced technology, so other brands will follow suit and compete. Eventually the biggest beneficiaries are consumers — everyone is competing to improve technology." Beyond cost-effectiveness and technological advantages, Chinese NEVs are also accelerating the global energy transition. The International Energy Agency estimated that the global electric vehicle fleet displaced about 1.7 million barrels of oil demand a day in 2025, with China accounting for roughly 1 million barrels a day. Chinese automakers' overseas expansion is currently in its early stages, far from reaching the level of globalization of traditional automotive powerhouses, Zheng from Roland Berger said. item.title: China to further prioritize AI-driven manufacturing
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-21
China to further prioritize AI-driven manufacturing Efforts urged to make nation's industrial chains more self-supporting, resilient China is putting artificial intelligence at the heart of its next manufacturing push, seeking to make factories smarter and critical supply chains more resilient, while keeping the world's largest manufacturing base plugged into global markets, officials, company executives and industry experts said on Sunday. The message was delivered as the 2026 World Manufacturing Convention opened on Sunday in Hefei, Anhui province. It came just days after China's top leadership called for sustained efforts to expand and strengthen advanced manufacturing, and make the country's industrial chains more self-supporting and risk-resilient at a national advanced manufacturing conference in Beijing last week. The timing of the two gatherings underscores a shift in the country's industrial priorities. Xin Guobin, vice-minister of industry and information technology, said at the Anhui convention that China will make a new generation of intelligent manufacturing a priority and push for the deeper integration of AI in manufacturing. "China will cultivate smart factories, develop open-source foundation models and industry-specific AI models, strengthen domestic manufacturing software and hardware, and accelerate the low-carbon transformation of factories," Xin said. That transition is particularly visible in Anhui. Liang Yanshun, Party secretary of Anhui, said that every minute, factories across the province produce about 190 home appliances, 50 laptop computers and four new energy vehicles. "Such momentum benefits from Anhui's decades of technological innovation and intelligent transformation. More and more Anhui-made products are setting sail overseas and benefiting consumers around the world," he said. One of the prime examples is ChangXin Memory Technologies. The Hefei-based memory chip maker said on Sunday that it has begun mass production of its fifth-generation, or G5, DRAM technology platform, which has reached the industry's most advanced manufacturing level. CXMT said that each wafer can now produce over 50 percent more usable memory chips than the previous-generation platform. Its 24GB LPDDR5X mobile memory chips based on the new platform are also in mass production and have been adopted by mainstream Chinese flagship smartphones. LPDDR5X is a type of high-speed, low-power memory chip widely used in premium smartphones, where higher capacity and faster data transfer are increasingly important for AI and other computing-intensive applications. Luo Xiaodong, vice-president of CXMT, said that the company had reduced the half-pitch of the active area in its memory array to 11.95 nanometers, putting CXMT close to the most advanced DRAM manufacturing technologies currently in mass production worldwide. The figure refers to the spacing between key structures inside a memory chip: the smaller the spacing, the more memory cells can be packed onto the same area of silicon. Latest data from the Anhui provincial government showed that during the 14th Five-Year Plan (2021-25) period, revenue from the province's large industrial companies climbed to 5.9 trillion yuan ($866 billion) from 3.8 trillion yuan, taking the province to fifth place nationwide. Carlos Magarinos, global chairman of the Global Alliance of SMEs and a former director-general of the United Nations Industrial Development Organization, said that Anhui had made a "profound impression", pointing to the rapid growth of sectors including new energy batteries and electronic information. Industry experts said that for China, the next manufacturing race is no longer simply about making more, but about making smarter and greener, and creating more advanced technology. Tian Jietang, head of the industrial economics department at the Development Research Center of the State Council, said: "China needs stronger advanced manufacturing capabilities and more resilient supply chains to cope with intensifying international competition."

item.title: Defending champion Hua Tian returns for his fourth Asiad
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-21
Share - WeChat
Chinese equestrian athlete Hua Tian is back at the 2026 Aichi-Nagoya 2026 Asian Games — and this time, he's in Tokyo for his fourth appearance. As the defending champion in eventing, Hua is aiming to stay competitive and fight for another medal with his horse Manjushri (also known as Bodhi). What has changed since the young rider first stepped onto the Asian Games stage? And how does he approach competition today? China Daily's Spotlight caught up with Hua ahead of the equestrian events to hear about his preparations and long-term goals with his horses. Copyright 1994 - .

item.title: Paving a win-win path for China and the West
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-21
Paving a win-win path for China and the West Share - WeChat
In a recent interview with China Daily's Global Lens, Alan Macfarlane, professor of social anthropology at the University of Cambridge, noted that the West has had a strong tendency toward binary thinking since ancient Greek times. In his view, this way of thinking profoundly distorts geopolitical and individual relations. "It isn't black and white and simplified. Collaboration and cooperation is good for everyone in facing major problems," he said. Macfarlane added that communication, travel, friendship, and better education of our children could help create a world free from binary opposition.

item.title: AI for good needs US-China cooperation
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-21
Turing Award winner: AI for good needs US-China cooperation Share - WeChat
The upcoming US visit by President Xi Jinping serves as a perfect opportunity for launching global AI cooperation led by China and the US, Joseph Sifakis, a Turing Award winner, told China Daily's Global Lens. Instead of letting tech giants dominate the response to transformation brought about by AI, China and the United States — as the two AI superpowers — should take the lead in fostering state-led cooperation, he said. Sifakis also advocated the building of a global AI governance framework, with the participation of Global South countries. Click on the video to watch more.

item.title: China's five initiatives address crucial issue for Global South
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-20
China's five initiatives address crucial issue for Global South Share - WeChat
China proposed five initiatives to deepen BRICS cooperation during the 18th BRICS Leaders' Meeting in New Delhi, India: the open source and inclusive AI initiative, the trade and investment facilitation initiative, the digital industry cooperation initiative, the intelligent manufacturing cooperation initiative, and the science and technology talent development initiative. Tian Li, director of the Internet Development Research Center at Peking University, said the five initiatives turn the Global South's shared aspiration for equitable development into concrete, actionable cooperation plans. They chart a clear course, offer an action guide, and provide a practical roadmap for BRICS countries as they usher in a shared future.
